# Results — Study 320 (Russell-Reconstitution) on the real IWM tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The front-run rule — buy the
small-cap index ETF at the close **5 sessions before** the late-June Russell reconstitution
Friday, sell on the reconstitution close — run on IWM (iShares Russell 2000) daily bars,
2000–2025. Each per-year window is pinned against the unconditional distribution of all
rolling 5-session block returns (and a same-month June control), with a one-sample t-test,
a Newey-West HAC t on the excess, and a 10,000-draw permutation test. As-of **2026-06-17**;
match the fingerprint to confirm you hold the same tape.*

## Data stamp

| Ticker | Window | Days | Fingerprint |
|---|---|--:|---|
| IWM | 2000-05-26 → 2026-06-17 | 6,553 | `ec8b35339b52` |

26 reconstitution events (2000–2025), one per year. The reconstitution calendar
(effective Fridays) is hardcoded in [`russell_reconstitution/data.py`](../russell_reconstitution/data.py)
from the FTSE Russell US-index recon schedule.

## The headline — IWM, 5-session run-up, gross

| Window | n | mean | excess vs baseline | up-rate | one-sample *t* vs base | HAC *t* (excess) | perm *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **5-session run-up** | 26 | +0.579% | **+36.4 bps** | 61.5% | +0.68 | **+0.89** | 0.55 |
| Reconstitution-day | 26 | +0.035% | ≈0 | 57.7% | −0.05 | −0.05 | 0.97 |
| 5-session post (give-back) | 26 | +0.018% | ≈0 | — | −0.33 | −0.33 | 0.55 |

- The run-up window does drift **up** (+0.58% over five sessions, up 62% of years) — but so
  does the small-cap ETF in general: the unconditional five-session block averages +0.22%.
  The **excess is +36 bps with HAC *t* = +0.89** — nowhere near the desk's |t| ≥ 2 hurdle.
- The reconstitution Friday itself and the give-back week are both **indistinguishable from
  zero**. The famous closing-auction volume spike moves a lot of *shares*, not the *price*.
- Against the **same-month (June) baseline** the excess is essentially unchanged (+35.3 bps,
  HAC *t* = +0.87, perm *p* = 0.53) — it is not even a "June vs the rest of the year" effect.

## It is not a window-length artefact either

| Run-up length | excess (bps) | HAC *t* | perm *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 1 session | −1.0 | −0.05 | 0.97 |
| 3 sessions | +57.0 | +1.74 | 0.25 |
| 5 sessions | +36.4 | +0.89 | 0.55 |
| 10 sessions | −41.5 | −0.86 | 0.62 |

No horizon clears |t| = 2. The 3-session window is the best of the bunch (*t* = +1.74) and
is itself a reminder that you can always find the most flattering window in a tiny sample —
it still does not clear the bar, and the 1- and 10-session windows are flat or negative.

## Sub-periods — no stable effect

| Period | n | mean (bps) | excess (bps) | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 2000–2008 | 9 | +67.4 | +45.9 | +0.72 |
| 2009–2016 | 8 | −18.4 | −39.9 | −0.90 |
| 2017–2025 | 9 | +116.2 | +94.7 | +1.50 |

The sign flips across thirds and no third clears |t| = 2. There is no durable, repeatable
run-up — just three small, noisy samples.

## Could you trade it? — the front-run rule (IWM, 5-session run-up, net)

Buy at the close 5 sessions before reconstitution Friday, sell on the event close, once a
year; 1 bp one-way (2 bps round-trip) on NAV.

| | per event | compounded (26 events) | annual |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Gross | +57.9 bps | ×1.151 | — |
| Net (2 bps round-trip) | +55.9 bps | ×1.145 | ~**+0.52%/yr** |

Costs are *not* the binding constraint (the trade is one round-trip a year). The binding
constraint is that there is **no statistically distinguishable edge to harvest**: a +0.5%/yr
contribution sitting in cash 360 days, built on an effect with HAC *t* = +0.89, is a sliver
of noise. And it dies even faster in practice — the predictable flow is exactly what
arbitrageurs, index funds' trade-scheduling, and the reconstitution's own multi-day
transition windows have competed away.

## Synthetic positive control — the engine is a faithful (but n-limited) detector

On the deterministic synthetic tape (same 26-event calendar) the engine recovers a planted
run-up premium **only when it is large**, because n = 26 windows is a low-power sample:

| Planted premium (bps/day) | excess (bps) | HAC *t* | perm *p* | detected? |
|---|--:|--:|--:|:--:|
| 0 | +21.8 | +0.25 | 0.70 | no (null) |
| 5 | +41.5 | +0.47 | 0.47 | no |
| 10 | +61.1 | +0.70 | 0.29 | no |
| 20 | +100.6 | +1.14 | 0.08 | no |
| 40 | +180.0 | +2.03 | 0.002 | yes |

The harness stays quiet at premium = 0 and only fires once the planted run-up reaches
~40 bps/day (~200 bps cumulative over five sessions). That is the honest reading of the
real tape: **at n = 26 a front-run edge would have to be enormous to be detectable, and the
real +36 bps cumulative excess is an order of magnitude below the detection floor.** The
synthetic is a machinery proof only; it never backs the Signal stamp.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** IWM 5-session run-up excess +36 bps, HAC *t* = +0.89; reconstitution
  day and give-back ≈ 0; same-month control unchanged; sign flips across sub-periods; no
  run-up length clears |t| = 2. Indistinguishable from noise on the real tape.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Even taken at face value the rule contributes ~+0.5%/yr while in
  cash 360 days — and there is no significant edge underneath it. The forced flow is real;
  the *price* impact you could capture is not.
- **Front-runnable? — NOT SUPPORTED.** The predictable, one-directional reconstitution flow
  is famous, but on the index ETF the price is already efficient by the time you could trade
  it. Big volume, no harvestable drift.
